summary: Psalm 20 begins as a communal prayer for someone facing trouble, asking Yahweh to answer, help, remember offerings, and grant the person's plans. The voice then shifts to confidence that Yahweh saves his anointed, contrasting trust in God's name with trust in chariots and horses. It ends with a brief plea: “Save, Yahweh!”
whyItMatters: This chapter shows royal and communal prayer joined together: the people pray for the anointed one, and their confidence rests on Yahweh rather than military strength. Within Psalms, it is one example of prayer shaped for public worship and crisis.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but Psalms headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much historical detail each heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; one date for the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: The psalm speaks from a setting of trouble, sacrifice, Zion, and confidence before conflict, but it does not narrate one specific event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a heading for the Chief Musician and the performance marker “Selah.”

outline.heading: Opening Prayer in Trouble
outline.note: The community asks Yahweh to answer, protect, and send help from the sanctuary and Zion.

outline.heading: Offerings and Desire
outline.note: The prayer asks Yahweh to remember offerings, accept sacrifice, and grant the person's desire and counsel.

outline.heading: Shared Confidence
outline.note: The speakers anticipate triumph in salvation and raise banners in God's name.

outline.heading: Yahweh Saves His Anointed
outline.note: A single voice declares confidence that Yahweh answers his anointed from holy heaven.

outline.heading: Trust Compared
outline.note: The psalm contrasts trust in chariots and horses with trust in Yahweh's name, then pictures the two outcomes.

outline.heading: Final Cry
outline.note: The chapter closes with a direct request for Yahweh to save and for the King to answer.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David. May Yahweh answer you in the day of trouble. May the name of the God of Jacob set you up on high,
keyVerses.why: The first verse gives the heading and frames the chapter as prayer for help in trouble.

keyVerses.text: Now I know that Yahweh saves his anointed. He will answer him from his holy heaven, with the saving strength of his right hand.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the shift from request to confidence and names the person prayed for as Yahweh's anointed.

keyVerses.text: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust in the name of Yahweh our God.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's clearest contrast: military resources are set beside trust in Yahweh's name.

keyVerses.text: Save, Yahweh! Let the King answer us when we call!
keyVerses.why: The final line gathers the chapter into a short cry for rescue and response.

themes: prayer in the day of trouble

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: Most of the chapter sounds like a group praying for someone else: “May Yahweh answer you” and “we will set up our banners.” Verse 6 shifts to “Now I know,” which may be an individual voice within the worship setting. The final verse returns to “us,” so the chapter keeps the community in view.

questions.question: Who is the “anointed” in verse 6?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name the person directly, but “his anointed” points to someone set apart for a special role, and the closing line mentions “the King.” In the psalm's first setting, many readers understand this as the king for whom the people are praying. Later Jewish and Christian readers may connect royal language with messianic hope, but that is reception beyond what the chapter itself spells out.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 3 after the request that Yahweh remember offerings and accept sacrifice. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker, so it is best not to assign it a precise meaning. Its presence reminds readers that this poem belonged to voiced or musical worship.

questions.question: What are the sanctuary and Zion doing in the prayer?
questions.answer: The prayer asks Yahweh to send help “from the sanctuary” and support “from Zion.” In Psalms, many poems are oriented toward Jerusalem and temple worship, and this chapter uses that worship-centered language. The verse does not require readers to reconstruct the exact ceremony behind it.

questions.question: Why does the psalm mention offerings and burned sacrifice?
questions.answer: Verse 3 asks Yahweh to remember “all your offerings” and accept “your burned sacrifice.” The psalm connects prayer for rescue with worship already offered, but it does not explain the details of the sacrifices. The point within the chapter is that the worshiper seeks God's favorable response before trouble or conflict.

questions.question: Does verse 4 mean God grants every desire?
questions.answer: Verse 4 is a blessing or request: “May he grant you your heart’s desire, and fulfill all your counsel.” It is not written as a universal guarantee detached from the chapter's setting. The surrounding lines keep the desire inside prayer to Yahweh, communal worship, and dependence on God's saving help.

questions.question: Why contrast chariots and horses with Yahweh's name?
questions.answer: Chariots and horses are images of military strength in verse 7. The speakers do not deny that such resources exist; they say their trust is elsewhere. Verse 8 then pictures the result as one side falling while the speakers rise and stand upright.

questions.question: What does “the name of Yahweh” mean here?
questions.answer: The phrase points to Yahweh as known and called upon, not to a magic formula. The chapter speaks of the “name of the God of Jacob,” “the name of our God,” and “the name of Yahweh our God.” Those repeated phrases tie rescue, banners, and trust to God's identity rather than to human strength.

questions.question: Is this psalm mainly private or public?
questions.answer: The chapter has personal language, but the repeated “we” and “us” make the public setting hard to miss. It sounds like a community praying for a leader or anointed figure in a time of danger. That public voice fits the broader Psalms collection, where individuals, leaders, choirs, and assemblies all speak before God.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that connects the psalm with musical or worship use; the exact ancient performance setting is not recoverable from this chapter alone.
The place named in verse 2 as the source from which support is requested; in Psalms, Zion is closely associated with Jerusalem and worship.
A preserved performance marker in verse 3 whose exact instruction is uncertain.
The person Yahweh saves in verse 6; in this chapter the term is linked with the royal language of “the King” in verse 9.
Military equipment named in verse 7 as something some people trust in, contrasted with trust in Yahweh's name.
The signs the speakers say they will set up in God's name when they triumph in salvation.
